findings.where: Nav bar lockup and hero mark (every place the logo appears)
findings.fault: The logo is recoloured. The aqueduct is drawn in the tile's near-black 'cut' (#2A2925) instead of the logo grey #404040, and the 'MMM INFRA' wordmark is dark instead of the logo blue #0070C0. The direction has no version of the logo that works on this ground: the logo blue sits close to the granite's lightness, so the full-colour logo would not stand off this mid-grey. The direction can only carry the logo by changing it.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose brand sheet keeps the logo (client value 7) and whose blue wordmark is what visitors know from his current site and LinkedIn. A returning visitor who knows the blue mark may also take this for a different firm. The house rule is to change the version or the ground, never the logo's colours, and to make a new version only with the client's yes.

findings.where: Hero headline 'MARK · M · MOSELEY / INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR'
findings.fault: The name and the role are set at the same size, colour and weight, so the two lines read as one run: 'Mark M Moseley Infrastructure Advisor', which can read like a firm's name. The interpuncts make it worse. The lone 'M' between two dots reads as a stray letter or another arch-M rather than a middle initial, and the dot in 'INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR' splits one job title into two words.
findings.who_objects: The bank official, who has to work out on first glance whether this is a person or a firm and what his role is. That slows the 5-second read the hero exists for.

findings.where: Whole page: hero name, article title, motion title, type specimen, the texture's capital M, the palette's AA swatch and the 'Write to Mark' button
findings.fault: Minium red is both the colour of every heading and the fill of the one action. The direction's own rule is 'one accent only, and it flows to the action', and the house reserves the primary action's colour for the action. With the large red name right above it, the button is not the strongest red thing in view. The red-filled 'AA' swatch (static) also has the button's look: Cinzel caps in lime on a minium box.
findings.who_objects: The visitor scanning for the next step, because the red headings compete with the one button for the eye. Lower on the page, red no longer means 'act here'.

findings.where: Article specimen, the boxed pull quote with dovetail handles (and the hero button it copies)
findings.fault: The tabula ansata is the shape of the only button, and the static pull quote takes the same shape: a framed tablet with triangular handles. Next to the filled red button, the outlined quote reads as an outlined, secondary button on the same ladder, so one shape means two functions. On the phone, the solid black wedges are the heaviest thing in the article and pull the eye off the text.
findings.who_objects: A reader of an article page, who may tap the quote expecting it to go somewhere. Once quotes share the shape, a visitor also has less reason to take the button's shape as 'this acts'. This was decided in the direction card, so it goes to the founder.

findings.where: Article specimen, the closing row 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the 'Abundance' Challenge · Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF'
findings.fault: A different lecture's title, from 2026, sits under an article from 2024 with no label. A reader cannot tell whether it is the PDF of this article, a related talk or the next post. The 'PDF' tag also suggests it opens a file directly rather than a page about the talk.
findings.who_objects: The official checking Mark's publications, who wants to know what they are opening, and who on a work machine may not want a surprise download.

findings.where: Article specimen title and dateline (Cinzel caps headings sitewide)
findings.fault: Cinzel has no lowercase, so every heading is tracked red capitals. The short specimen title already runs to three lines on desktop and phone. Mark's real titles, such as 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the 'Abundance' Challenge', would make tall slabs of capitals that are slow to read. On the phone the dateline wraps, leaving '2024' alone on its own line.
findings.who_objects: Readers skimming an article list, since long all-caps titles are read letter by letter. Angélique, too, cannot shorten Mark's titles when she adds a post (client value 9).

findings.where: Hero, 'Write to Mark' button (and no footer or contact line anywhere on the page)
findings.fault: The only contact route is a mailto button. Mark's email address is never shown as text.
findings.who_objects: The bank official on a managed work machine where mailto opens nothing or the wrong client. They cannot copy an address to send from their own system, so the page's one action fails silently.

findings.where: Whole tile, no place for Mark's photograph
findings.fault: Mark is never seen. The tile has no portrait and no labelled stand-in for one, so it does not show how a real photograph of him would sit on the grey stone next to the red capitals.
findings.who_objects: The visitor, who looks for a real named face before writing to a solo advisor. Mark, too, has listed 'the man himself — seen and heard' among the values every direction must answer.

findings.where: Whole page ground (granite #B8B5AD), with the hero's monumental red inscription
findings.fault: Until the stone photograph arrives, a flat mid-grey ground with no texture reads as greyed-out or dimmed rather than as stone. Big carved red capitals over it make the first screen feel like a memorial plaque or a heritage site, not an approachable personal advisor.
findings.who_objects: The visitor's first impression of something dim and formal. Mark asked for a personal, approachable advisor and confidence without grand claims (values 1 and 6), and none of his four suggested grounds is a mid-grey.

findings.where: Motion sketch, the closing note and the code strings
findings.fault: The tile shows internal scaffolding to its reader: a repository path ('docs/research/animation-length.md F5/F12'), a ticket number ('#13') and 'units (≈290 px)'. These are set in a monospace face larger than the text around them, which brings in a third typeface the type pair does not name.
findings.who_objects: Mark, the lay reader who will judge this tile. He gets developer references he cannot use, and the stray face weakens the claim that the look is one type pair.

findings.where: Desktop tile layout: under the article specimen, under the palette, and the gap between the Cinzel and Alegreya specimens
findings.fault: The two columns end at very different heights. A large empty block sits under the article while the motion-sketch box runs on, and the palette column stops well above the texture caption, so the lower half of the page looks unfinished and lopsided.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the founder judging the tile as a whole, since the gaps read as missing content rather than as chosen space.

findings.fault: A static label is set in the button's Cinzel tracked capitals inside its own outlined box, so it looks like a small outlined button. The type pair's own note says Cinzel is for headings, the nav and the button only.
findings.who_objects: A reader who clicks it expecting something to happen. It also breaks the tile's own type rule.
